strengths: Strong reported mathematical reasoning performance across several model sizes. AgentMath-8B achieves 89.8%, 84.7%, and 71.3% on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, respectively, outperforming the listed similarly sized baselines.
The end-to-end pipeline addresses practical challenges in synthesizing executable demonstrations and training agents with long trajectories and frequent tool interactions.

The evaluation includes useful controlled evidence: a same-backbone, 20k-example text-versus-tool comparison, progressive data-refinement ablations, data scaling experiments, and SFT-to-RL improvements across three model sizes.

The appendix provides synthesis prompts, dataset construction details, training settings, and evaluation parameters. The partial-rollout study reports substantial time savings with approximately preserved benchmark accuracy.
weaknesses: The claimed methodological novelty is insufficiently established. Interleaved code execution, outcome-based RL, and masking environment outputs substantially overlap with acknowledged approaches such as ReTool and ToRL. The paper does not isolate its algorithmic contribution through matched implementations of these methods, and the introduction's assertion that RL-based tool-strategy optimization remains unexplored conflicts with its own related-work discussion.

The main comparisons do not establish matched training data, inference budgets, or tool resources, and it is unclear which baseline results were reproduced versus imported. The controlled text-only comparison uses 20k SFT examples rather than the full 316k-example pipeline. Evaluation is restricted to three small competition benchmarks, without confidence intervals or training-seed variation; this particularly limits interpretation of the modest 30B gains over Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507.

The data-consistency verifier has a concrete correctness weakness: Appendix A.6.3 treats numerical values differing by up to 1.0 as equivalent, including after converting percentages to decimals, and ignores information absent from one compared text. These rules can accept mathematically consequential discrepancies between simulated and actual execution outputs. Exact final-answer checking does not establish the correctness of intermediate supervision, and no audit quantifies this issue.

The reward does not substantiate the claimed tool-use efficiency. It adds a capped term linear in invocation count, but alpha, beta, and the cap are unspecified. With positive beta, it rewards additional calls rather than economical use. There is no correctness-only reward ablation or accuracy-versus-cost analysis. Likewise, rising tool counts do not establish optimal strategies, and an isolated debugging example cannot establish emergent self-correction when correction trajectories are explicitly included in SFT.

Partial-rollout optimization is underspecified. Trajectories can span policy updates, while the stated GRPO objective assumes sampling from a single old policy. The paper does not explain behavior-policy probability tracking, staleness handling, or group completion across segments. Algorithm 1 also leaves experience-buffer lifetime and retention of unsampled unfinished tasks unclear. These details matter for both reproducibility and the validity of the learning procedure.

The efficiency evidence does not fully support end-to-end claims. Table 6 omits GPU hardware/count, detailed workload configuration, and comparisons with strong existing asynchronous systems. Time per step under segmentation needs normalization by completed trajectories or effective training work. Separately, 400 versus 1,600 optimization steps is not a wall-clock comparison, and shorter generated text does not account for interpreter latency or CPU cost.

Material reporting inconsistencies weaken confidence: the conclusion reports 78.9% HMMT25 accuracy for AgentMath-30B-A3B, versus 73.8% in the abstract and tables. The main text gives the corresponding Qwen baseline as 74.3%, versus 71.4% in Table 1, which changes the direction of that comparison. The appendix's symmetric, trajectory-normalized GRPO equation also does not reflect the claimed asymmetric clipping and token-level loss.

strengths: Strong reported results across several model sizes, particularly AgentMath-8B at 89.8%, 84.7%, and 71.3% on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25. Table 5 also shows substantial improvements from SFT to RL.

The automated trajectory-conversion pipeline is practically useful. The matched 20k-example text-versus-tool comparison and progressive refinement ablations provide concrete evidence that tool augmentation and data cleaning improve performance.

The infrastructure addresses a relevant bottleneck in long-context agent training. Tables 6–7 report incremental timing improvements and approximately preserved accuracy across partial-rollout configurations.
The appendix supplies synthesis prompts, data sources and filtering procedures, major training hyperparameters, and evaluation settings, including 32 samples per problem.
weaknesses: The claimed methodological novelty is insufficiently established. Interleaved code execution, outcome-based RL, environment-token masking, and GRPO/DAPO adaptations substantially overlap with cited approaches such as ReTool and ToRL. The paper itself describes prior RL-based strategic tool use, undermining its assertion that this direction remains unexplored. Controlled comparisons against these methods using the same backbone, data, and budgets are missing.

The consistency verifier has a concrete technical weakness: Appendix A.6.3 treats numerical values as equivalent whenever their absolute difference is at most 1.0 and ignores information present in only one text. This can accept materially incorrect mathematical feedback, especially after percentages are normalized. Authentic execution therefore does not establish the claimed contextual consistency; a verifier-error audit or stricter-check ablation is needed.

The reward does not substantiate efficient or optimal tool use. Section 2.3.2 makes the tool bonus depend on invocation count; with positive beta it rewards additional calls until saturation, without measuring usefulness or cost. The values of alpha, beta, and the cap are unspecified, and there is no correctness-only reward comparison. Rising invocation counts are consequently weak evidence of improved strategy.

Important causal claims lack targeted evaluation. Budget increases coincide with continued RL, without fixed-budget controls. Self-correction is explicitly included in SFT, so a qualitative debugging example cannot establish that it emerges through RL. Quantitative recovery rates and an RL comparison with and without correction demonstrations are absent.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Tables 6–7 omit GPU type/count and sufficient workload accounting to establish resource-matched comparisons. Partial rollouts can change how much completed experience contributes to each update, but completed trajectories and tokens per step are not reported. Separately, fewer optimization steps and shorter outputs do not establish lower total cost when tool execution and data synthesis are excluded.

The partial-rollout optimization procedure is underspecified. Algorithm 1 resumes unfinished trajectories across policy updates, whereas the stated GRPO objective assumes sampling from a single old policy. Behavior-policy bookkeeping, policy staleness, experience-buffer reuse, and completion of rollout groups are not explained sufficiently to assess or reproduce the learning procedure.

Evaluation is limited to three competition benchmarks, with unclear provenance and budget matching for the many baseline scores. There are no uncertainty estimates or independent training runs; 32 generations per problem do not resolve uncertainty from the small benchmark problem sets. This matters particularly for the 30B model's relatively modest gains over Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507.

Central results contain unresolved inconsistencies: the conclusion reports 78.9% HMMT25 accuracy for AgentMath-30B-A3B, versus 73.8% in the abstract and tables. Section 3.1 gives its Qwen3 comparator 74.3%, versus 71.4% in Table 1; the prose value would reverse the claimed HMMT25 advantage. These discrepancies require correction before the headline comparisons can be trusted.

strengths: Strong reported mathematical reasoning performance across several model sizes. AgentMath-8B achieves 89.8%, 84.7%, and 71.3% on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, respectively, substantially exceeding several relevant baselines.

The integrated data synthesis and training pipeline addresses practical challenges in tool-augmented reasoning, including executable demonstrations, authentic interpreter feedback, debugging examples, and long interactive rollouts.

The evaluation includes useful controlled evidence: the same-backbone, 20k-data comparison favors tool augmentation; Table 3 examines progressive data refinement; Table 5 demonstrates improvements from RL across three model sizes.

The systems experiments provide component-wise timing measurements and examine the accuracy–efficiency tradeoff of partial rollouts. The appendix also supplies synthesis prompts, dataset construction details, training hyperparameters, and explicit benchmark decontamination procedures.
weaknesses: The claimed novel agentic RL paradigm is insufficiently distinguished from existing work. Interleaved execution, outcome-based RL, interpreter-token masking, and synthesis followed by RL closely resemble the cited ToRL and ReTool approaches. The paper acknowledges these precedents but does not establish which algorithmic advance, beyond integration and scale, explains its gains.

The main comparisons do not isolate the proposed method from differences in backbone, training data, and computation. The controlled text-only experiment uses only 20k SFT examples, whereas headline results use approximately 316k. A full-scale matched text-only baseline and a same-backbone implementation of a strong tool-RL baseline are needed. Baseline provenance and whether all results follow the stated inference protocol are also unclear.

The tool reward does not substantiate the claimed optimization of efficient tool use. It depends on invocation count without measuring usefulness or cost; a positive count coefficient rewards additional calls until saturation. Values for alpha, beta, and the reward cap are unspecified, and there is no accuracy-only reward ablation. Increased tool frequency therefore cannot establish improved strategic decision-making.

The consistency verifier in Appendix A.6.3 treats numerical differences up to 1.0 as equivalent, including for final conclusions, and ignores non-overlapping information. This can accept materially incorrect intermediate computations in exact mathematics. Although benchmark answers use a separate verifier, the synthesis pipeline's high-quality-data claim needs a stricter consistency check and an empirical error audit.

The efficiency claims lack essential controls. Table 6 omits GPU types/counts and sufficiently precise workload specifications, while the 128-node execution cluster's resource cost is not incorporated. Fewer training steps and shorter outputs do not establish proportional compute or latency savings when tool execution adds overhead. Comparison against a strong existing asynchronous RL system is missing.

Partial rollouts can span policy updates, but the treatment of mixed-policy trajectories, stored behavior probabilities, stale experience, and completed GRPO groups is not explained. These details matter for both reproducibility and the validity of the stated optimization objective.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence: self-correction is explicitly taught during SFT but described as emergent from RL without quantitative isolation; budget expansion is not compared with fixed-budget training; and modest 30B gains lack uncertainty estimates. Reporting is also inconsistent: the conclusion gives HMMT25 accuracy as 78.9%, whereas the main tables report 73.8%. Overall, the promising results do not yet resolve the novelty, attribution, and validation gaps required for acceptance.

strengths: Strong empirical results across model sizes and architectures. Beyond the main competition benchmarks, IMO-AnswerBench provides broader evidence: AgentMath-30B-A3B achieves 51.2% versus 41.4% for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507.

The appendix includes meaningful controlled comparisons. Matching ReTool’s backbone, teacher responses, training problems, and RL steps yields improvements from 67.0%/49.3% to 74.8%/56.6% on AIME24/25. A full-data, matched text-distillation baseline also supports the benefit of tool-augmented supervision.

Extensive ablations examine synthesis segmentation, refinement stages, training-data scale, reward design, and partial-rollout segmentation. Consistent SFT-to-RL improvements across Qwen and Llama backbones strengthen the empirical contribution.

The integrated training pipeline addresses a practical challenge in long-context tool-using RL. Cumulative systems ablations report substantial speedups, while segmentation experiments show approximately preserved downstream accuracy.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is overstated. Interleaved execution, outcome-based RL, and masking environmental tokens are established techniques, including in cited ReTool and ToRL work. The strongest contribution is the synthesis recipe and systems integration, rather than a fundamentally new agentic RL paradigm.

Evaluation independence is insufficiently established. Appendices A.13–A.16 explicitly use AIME24/25 performance to select segmentation, teacher, and reward settings, without clearly identifying a separate development set. No uncertainty estimates accompany the reported gains; repeated generations do not replace independent test problems or training-seed variability.

The 4–5× systems claim lacks sufficient experimental specification: GPU models/counts for the timing comparison, workload normalization, completed trajectories per update, and comparisons with modern asynchronous RL systems are unclear. Fewer training steps and generated tokens also do not establish end-to-end efficiency without accounting for tool execution and infrastructure costs.

Partial rollouts can span policy updates, but the treatment of mixed-policy trajectories, behavior-policy probabilities, staleness, and GRPO group completion is unspecified. Algorithm 1 and the generic GRPO objective do not adequately explain these implementation-critical details.

The tool reward increases with invocation count, so it encourages additional calls rather than directly rewarding efficiency. Appendix A.16 provides useful accuracy ablations but does not establish that calls are necessary or that the reward prevents redundant tool use. Claims of emergent self-correction also require stronger evidence because correction traces are explicitly included in SFT.

Contamination safeguards are useful but do not justify claims that leakage is eliminated. Earlier backbone release dates do not exclude contamination through later SFT/RL data or teacher responses, and removing the five nearest semantic neighbors provides no guarantee. Reporting also needs reconciliation: the conclusion gives 78.9% HMMT25 accuracy for the 30B model versus 73.8% in Table 1.

strengths: The strongest contribution is a practical, scalable recipe for tool-augmented mathematical reasoning. Segmented trajectory rewriting, execution-based refinement, and long-horizon RL produce substantial improvements across several model sizes and backbone families.

The appendix provides meaningful controlled comparisons. With the same backbone, teacher responses, and 316k training examples, tool-augmented SFT improves AIME24/AIME25 from 74.9/67.4 to 78.4/72.2 (Table 26). The matched ReTool comparison also favors AgentMath after both SFT and RL (Table 25), supporting a contribution beyond simply using stronger teachers or more data.

Evaluation extends beyond the three small headline benchmarks. On the 400-problem IMO-AnswerBench, RL improves the 8B model from 28.8 to 37.9 and the 30B-A3B model from 43.5 to 51.2. Additional Llama and Qwen2.5 experiments strengthen the evidence for generality.

Ablations cover synthesis segmentation, refinement stages, data volume, teacher selection, reward design, and rollout segmentation. The systems experiments report substantial latency reductions with approximately preserved accuracy, providing useful evidence for the engineering contribution.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is overstated. Interleaving reasoning with code execution, masking environment tokens, and applying outcome-based GRPO are already central to closely related work such as ReTool and ToRL. The paper is more convincing as a data-and-systems contribution than as a novel agentic RL paradigm; its introduction should reflect this distinction.

Evaluation independence and uncertainty need better treatment. Appendices A.13.1, A.14.4, and A.16 explicitly use AIME results to select segmentation length, teacher, and reward parameters, without clearly separating development and final test sets. Repeated decoding does not overcome the limited number of distinct problems, and confidence intervals or training-seed variability are not reported. Appendix A.15 mentions eight training runs but reports a selected checkpoint rather than their distribution.

Partial rollout training is underspecified. Algorithm 1 updates the policy while retaining unfinished trajectories, potentially mixing policy versions within a completed trajectory. The paper does not explain behavior-policy probability bookkeeping, staleness handling, or how GRPO groups are assembled when trajectories finish in different iterations. These details matter for both correctness and reproduction.

The efficiency claims exceed the available measurements. Tables 6 and 11 compare against a static synchronous baseline without sufficiently specifying hardware allocation, completed-trajectory throughput, or comparisons with contemporary asynchronous systems. Because segmentation changes work performed per iteration, time per step alone is insufficient. Likewise, fewer RL steps and fewer generated tokens do not directly establish proportional savings in total compute or inference latency once tool execution is included.

The tool reward encourages invocation count rather than resource efficiency: with positive beta, additional calls increase reward for correct answers until saturation. Table 27 supports a modest accuracy benefit, but does not demonstrate optimal tool use or avoidance of redundant calls. Similarly, examples of debugging do not establish emergent self-correction, especially because correction traces are explicitly injected during SFT.

Several claims and reporting details need correction. Earlier backbone release dates reduce pretraining-contamination risk but do not establish freedom from post-training overlap or overlap with original problems underlying rewritten benchmarks. The conclusion reports 78.9% HMMT25 accuracy for the 30B model, versus 73.8% in the main table, and the Qwen3-30B comparator differs between the table and prose. Despite extensive procedural descriptions, no accompanying implementation, checkpoints, or synthesized dataset are supplied in the manuscript, limiting verification of the complex pipeline.

strengths: Strong empirical results across model scales. AgentMath-8B achieves 89.8%, 84.7%, and 71.3% on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, respectively, substantially improving over its SFT initialization and competitive comparably sized models.

The appendix materially strengthens the evaluation: the 400-problem IMO-AnswerBench, additional Llama and Qwen2.5 backbones, and consistent SFT-to-RL improvements provide evidence beyond the small headline benchmarks. AgentMath-30B-A3B scores 51.2% on IMO-AnswerBench versus 41.4% for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507.

Useful controlled comparisons address attribution. Under matched problems, teacher responses, backbone, and training steps, AgentMath outperforms ReTool; a separate full-data text-only SFT control also supports the benefit of tool-augmented trajectories beyond teacher distillation alone.

The synthesis pipeline is practical and extensively investigated, including segmentation, execution verification, feedback alignment, correction examples, teacher selection, and data scaling. Prompts and substantial training details are provided.
The infrastructure targets a meaningful bottleneck. Cumulative timing measurements and partial-rollout experiments show substantial acceleration with approximately preserved benchmark accuracy.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated. Interleaved code execution, outcome-based RL, and learning tool-use strategies are already central to cited work such as ReTool and ToRL. The strongest contribution is the integrated synthesis and scaling recipe; describing agentic RL itself as a novel paradigm or previously unexplored is not justified.

Partial-rollout optimization is underspecified. Algorithm 1 updates the policy while retaining unfinished trajectories, potentially mixing behavior-policy versions within trajectories. The paper does not explain policy-version tracking, the appropriate importance-sampling denominators, or how complete GRPO groups are assembled when trajectories finish at different iterations. Appendix A.3 presents a conventional single-old-policy objective rather than resolving these implementation questions.

Efficiency evidence needs better normalization and reproducibility. The 4–5× result uses a static synchronous baseline without sufficiently specifying the accelerator configuration and completed trajectory/token workload for each timing condition. Modern asynchronous baselines are missing. Separately, fewer RL steps and fewer generated tokens do not establish proportional wall-clock or total-compute savings when tool execution and synthesis costs differ.

The positive tool-count bonus rewards additional calls, not computational efficiency or necessary calls. Appendix A.16 supports an accuracy benefit but does not establish efficient or optimal tool use. Likewise, qualitative debugging examples do not establish emergent self-correction, particularly because correction trajectories are explicitly included in SFT.

Statistical and evaluation controls remain incomplete. Repeated decoding reduces sampling noise but does not overcome the small number of distinct AIME/HMMT problems. Confidence intervals and training-run variability are absent; Appendix A.15 mentions eight training runs but reports a selected checkpoint without the distribution or a clearly specified validation set. Teacher, segmentation, and reward choices are also justified using headline benchmark performance.

Some claims and reporting require correction. Earlier backbone release dates do not eliminate contamination through later distillation or post-training, and removing the five closest training examples cannot guarantee semantic decontamination. The conclusion reports 78.9% HMMT25 accuracy for AgentMath-30B-A3B versus 73.8% in Table 1; the Qwen3-30B comparator is also inconsistent between the table and discussion. These issues weaken confidence in otherwise promising results.
